title: FDD Item 1: which company is offering the franchise?
seoTitle: FDD Item 1: Franchisor, Parents and Related Companies
description: A brand name and the company signing the franchise agreement can be different.
learningSummary: A brand name and the company signing the franchise agreement can be different. Item 1 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) identifies the franchisor and the specified related businesses, and describes the business being offered.

sections.heading: Identify the seller and the business
paragraphs: Item 1 covers the franchisor and specified parents, predecessors and affiliates. An affiliate is a related business under the item’s control test; a predecessor is a relevant earlier business. It also addresses the business background, offered operation, market and relevant industry-law context.
A reorganisation does not simply erase required history. Use the complete item to establish which companies and information belong in the disclosure.

sections.heading: Check who makes each important promise
paragraphs: Suppose a Swedish parent creates a U.S. seller while another group company owns the software. Saying “our group supports you” leaves a practical gap: does the seller have the rights and arrangements needed to provide that support?
Compare the named seller with the agreements for brand rights, software, fees and services. Parent ownership alone does not make the parent responsible for the subsidiary’s promises.

practicalOutput: Identify the seller and any other company needed to deliver the offer before describing group support to a prospect.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Specified franchisor, parents, predecessors and affiliates; control/history scope.
Business background, offered business, market and industry-law context.
Seller/rights owner/support obligations distinct; no assumed parent guarantee.

title: FDD Item 2: whose business experience must be explained?
seoTitle: FDD Item 2: Business Experience and Franchise Support
description: Item 2 describes the recent business experience of the people behind franchise sales and operations.
learningSummary: Item 2 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) describes the recent business experience of the people behind franchise sales and operations. A founder biography alone may leave out other people covered by the item.

sections.heading: Use the covered people’s five-year histories
paragraphs: The item covers relevant directors, principal officers and people with management responsibility for franchise sales or operations. It identifies their principal positions and employers over the last five years. Collect the real history for the covered people, rather than replacing it with a short brand story.

sections.heading: Branch experience and franchise support can differ
paragraphs: A successful branch director may never have trained independent owners or supported several regions. Their branch history belongs in the required biography; it does not by itself establish available time or experience for the support being sold.
Use the promised training and continuing services in Item 11 to judge that separate staffing question. Do not describe hoped-for experience as an existing qualification.

practicalOutput: Check the covered people and their five-year positions and employers; compare the support team with the actual services being offered.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Covered directors/principal officers/sales or operations managers.
Principal positions and employers over five years.
Required history distinct from optional delivery-capacity assessment; no invented professional qualifications.

title: FDD Item 3: reading the litigation history
seoTitle: FDD Item 3: Litigation, Allegations and Case Outcomes
description: A disclosed claim is not automatically a proven accusation.
learningSummary: A disclosed claim is not automatically a proven accusation. Read who is involved, what the proceeding concerns and whether it is pending, settled or decided before drawing a business conclusion.

sections.heading: Item 3 covers specified proceedings
paragraphs: The item specifies covered people and companies, claim categories and relevant periods. It includes specified pending matters, certain franchise-relationship actions and qualifying historical outcomes or orders. It is not a list of every disagreement.

Match the entity and proceeding to the prescribed item when preparing disclosure. A case with a similar company name, or any real case mentioned elsewhere on this site, is not automatically a required Item 3 entry.

sections.heading: Ask what the record actually establishes
paragraphs: A complaint states allegations. A settlement can end a dispute without a contested trial, but its admissions and obligations depend on its actual terms. A judgment must be read for what was decided and how; an amount ordered is not proof that the money was recovered.

If a dispute concerns promised support, compare that promise with the support you now offer and can deliver. Do not dismiss a pending claim as meaningless or present it as a finding of fraud. The linked court-record guide explains these record types.

practicalOutput: Read the identified complaint, order or settlement and establish the correct party and status before describing the dispute.
limitations: This explains how to read the specified litigation disclosure, not a complete disclosure-category checklist or a universal disputes search.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Specified parties/categories/periods; pending, relationship and qualifying historical matters.
Allegation versus admission/settlement/judgment; no collection finding.
Documented case does not establish mandatory Item3 coverage without party/category/period match.

title: FDD Item 4: bankruptcy history and a new U.S. seller
seoTitle: FDD Item 4: Bankruptcy History and the FDD Date
description: Item 4 covers specified bankruptcy histories, including relevant people and related companies, during the required ten-year period.
learningSummary: A new U.S. company does not erase the bankruptcy history that Item 4 requires. The item addresses specified people, companies and proceedings in the ten years before the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) date.

sections.heading: Check identity, role and dates
paragraphs: Coverage can include specified foreign insolvency proceedings as well as U.S. bankruptcy. An insolvency proceeding deals with financial distress under the relevant law. Check the actual entity or person, their relevant role, dates and outcome against the prescribed item; a shared name or general search result is insufficient.

sections.heading: Read today’s finances separately
paragraphs: An older proceeding involving a covered person or business may need disclosure even though the U.S. seller is new. Its presence does not by itself predict the seller’s failure, and its absence is not a complete financial assessment.
For present resources and support commitments, read the relevant financial statements and guarantees under Item 21.

practicalOutput: Check the required ten-year history using the dated FDD, then assess current finances through the separate financial disclosures.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Ten years before FDD date, covered parties/roles and foreign proceedings.
History distinct from present capacity; no failure prediction or no-history assurance.

title: FDD Item 5: initial fees and other pre-opening commitments
seoTitle: FDD Item 5: Initial Fees, Payees and Refund Terms
description: The entry fee may be only one payment before opening.
learningSummary: The entry fee may be only one payment before opening. Item 5 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) covers specified payments and commitments to the franchisor or its affiliates, including the relevant refund conditions.

sections.heading: Read every covered payment, not just the headline fee
paragraphs: A cleaning offer might include an initial fee, software setup paid to a related company and training charges. Identify the recipient, amount or formula, when the commitment arises and the stated refund conditions. Where fees differ, the required range or formula and the reasons for differences matter.
The actual offer supplies the refund policy. This example creates no right to recover a payment if a site is rejected, training stops or the launch is cancelled.

sections.heading: Check timing before taking money
paragraphs: Calling a payment a reservation fee does not determine whether a disclosure duty applies. Check its real purpose, recipient and timing before collecting it.
Item 7 addresses the broader opening investment. Rent and third-party fit-out do not disappear because they are outside the headline fee.

practicalOutput: Compare the offer’s pre-opening commitments and refund terms with the agreements, broader investment estimate and disclosure timetable.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Covered fees/payments/commitments before opening to franchisor/affiliate.
Nonuniform range/formula/factors and actual refund conditions, no invented refund entitlement.
Separate early-payment disclosure timing and Item7 broader initial investment.

title: FDD Item 6: what the royalty leaves out
seoTitle: FDD Item 6: Other Fees, Royalties and Payment Triggers
description: A royalty percentage does not show the operator’s full fee burden.
learningSummary: A royalty percentage does not show the operator’s full fee burden. Item 6 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) explains covered fees, their amount or formula, when they are due and the conditions attached.

sections.heading: Check regular and event-based charges
paragraphs: The table covers fees paid to the franchisor or affiliates, or imposed or collected for third parties. The actual offer may include technology, training, audit, transfer or renewal charges as well as royalties; it does not follow that every brand charges each one.

For a percentage of gross sales, read the contractual sales definition. It may differ from cash collected or accounting revenue. Where a fee may increase, the disclosed increase formula or maximum matters too. Keep fees distinct from independent taxes.

sections.heading: A percentage needs a defined base
paragraphs: Fictional example: a 6% royalty on a contract-defined monthly sales amount of $10,000 is $600. That answers one fee line. Add the actual technology and event-based charges separately, and use their payment dates when considering cash needs.

practicalOutput: Read each fee’s base, due event and increase terms before using the royalty percentage in the operating budget.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Franchisor/affiliate and imposed/collected third-party fees; amounts/formulas/dates/conditions.
Defined gross sales and increase formula or maximum; fees distinct from taxes.
Fictional6%of$10k=$600; not profitability/collection forecast.

title: FDD Item 7: will the opening budget leave enough cash?
seoTitle: FDD Item 7: Estimated Initial Investment and Opening Cash
description: Item 7 estimates the initial investment, including relevant additional funds for the initial operating period.
learningSummary: Item 7 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) estimates the initial investment, including relevant additional funds for the initial operating period. The entry fee alone does not show how much cash the proposed unit needs.

sections.heading: Read the estimate’s assumptions
paragraphs: The prescribed table includes relevant costs, payment methods, timing and recipients. Its additional-funds category addresses other required expenses before operations and during the stated initial operating period, with the estimate’s basis explained. The rule describes a reasonable initial period as at least three months or a reasonable period for the industry.

Your actual site, wages, suppliers and opening date may differ. Check what the allowance already includes before adding another manager cost or reserve; equally, do not assume an excluded cost is covered.

sections.heading: Opening costs and operating cash are different
paragraphs: Fictional example: the owners have $100,000 and spend $80,000 establishing the business. The $20,000 left covers only two months if the operating cash gap is $10,000 per month. A delay or slower customer payment changes the result.
These are invented figures, not typical costs. Replace assumptions with actual quotes and dates, keeping missing costs visible rather than treating them as zero.

practicalOutput: Compare the disclosed estimate with the actual payment dates, opening assumptions and cash available after setup.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Item7 categories/payment method/timing/payees and stated additional-funds basis.
Reasonable initial period at least3months or reasonable industry period.
Fictional$100k−$80k=$20k; $10k gap two months; no typical cost/forecast and no double counting.

title: FDD Item 8: can the operator use a local supplier?
seoTitle: FDD Item 8: Purchasing Restrictions and Approved Suppliers
description: Required products and approved suppliers affect operating costs. Item 8 explains purchasing restrictions and the related supplier interests and benefits.
learningSummary: Required products and approved suppliers can affect the cost and reliability of a U.S. unit. Item 8 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) explains the purchasing restrictions, alternative-approval process and relevant supplier benefits behind the offer.

sections.heading: Read the requirement and approval process
paragraphs: The item addresses required purchases or leases, approved suppliers, specifications, approval procedures and relevant revenues or benefits received by the brand or related companies. Include arrangements used in practice, not just restrictions written into the main agreement.

sections.heading: Compare a substitute before promising savings
paragraphs: Suppose a European maintenance brand requires a cleaning chemical and the U.S. operator proposes a cheaper local product. Check the performance specification and stated supplier-approval route. Compare delivered costs, including relevant transport/import costs, rather than unit price alone.

Brand approval is a private decision. Product, import, labelling or use requirements come from the relevant authorities and depend on the actual product and activity. A preferred home supplier is not the only lawful source merely because the brand prefers it.

practicalOutput: Check the stated alternative-supplier process and the delivered cost of the actual products needed for the U.S. service.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Required purchases/leases, specifications/approval route and supplier benefits; actual practice.
Private approval separate from government product/use/import requirements.
Delivered cost and supply continuity; no automatic local-substitute or sole-lawful-source finding.

title: FDD Item 9: follow the obligation to the contract
seoTitle: FDD Item 9: Franchisee Obligations and Contract References
description: Item 9 points from the principal operator obligations to the relevant agreements and FDD items.
learningSummary: Item 9 points from the principal operator obligations to the relevant agreements and Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) items. The table helps you find the terms; its short labels do not contain all the conditions.

sections.heading: Follow one training entry
paragraphs: A training reference might lead you to the agreement and the participation information in Item 15. Read those provisions to establish who must attend, when, who pays and what applies if a manager is replaced. This guide supplies no actual brand’s clause, so those answers cannot be filled in here.

sections.heading: Doing the work and owing the obligation differ
paragraphs: An owner may employ a manager to carry out a task. That internal assignment does not automatically change the party responsible under the franchise agreement.
Keep independent government duties in view too. A contract’s allocation does not decide every employment, tax or licensing obligation.

practicalOutput: Follow the relevant Item 9 reference into the actual provision before assigning the work or budgeting its cost.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Principal franchisee obligations cross-reference actual agreement and FDDitems.
No actual clause/attendance/cost/replacement terms supplied.
Internal delegation does not change contractual responsibility or settle independent duties.

title: FDD Item 10: financing now, repayments later
seoTitle: FDD Item 10: Franchisor Financing and Repayment Terms
description: Financing can reduce the cash paid at opening while leaving a debt to repay.
learningSummary: Financing can reduce the cash paid at opening while leaving a debt to repay. Item 10 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) explains covered financing offered directly or indirectly through the franchisor, its agents or affiliates.

sections.heading: Read what repayment commits you to
paragraphs: Relevant terms include interest, charges, repayment, security, guarantees, default consequences and relevant assignment or lender benefits. Security means property or rights supporting the creditor’s claim; a guarantee is another party’s promise to answer for the obligation.

Read who owes the money and what the financing documents define as default. Also check whether another creditor can take over the debt and what relevant benefit the brand receives from the financing arrangement.

sections.heading: Test the payment dates against opening
paragraphs: If part of an opening payment is deferred, it has not automatically become a discount. Put the actual repayment dates and charges alongside wages, rent and other cash needs.
Do not assume a delayed opening delays repayment. The financing agreement supplies the answer; the brand’s involvement does not remove the consequences in its guarantee or security documents.

practicalOutput: Read the financing, security and guarantee documents together and test the actual repayments against the opening timetable.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Covered direct/indirect franchisor/agent/affiliate financing.
Interest/charges/repayment/security/guarantee/default/assignment/benefits.
Deferral not automaticallydiscount; no assumed interest rate or payment deferral on openingdelay.

title: FDD Item 11: what support are you promising?
seoTitle: FDD Item 11: Assistance, Advertising, Systems and Training
description: “Training and ongoing support” can mean very different services.
learningSummary: “Training and ongoing support” can mean very different services. Item 11 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) explains specified assistance, advertising, computer systems and training, with the relevant agreement references.

sections.heading: Explain the service and its conditions
paragraphs: Separate pre-opening assistance from continuing support. Identify what is promised, what depends on conditions and what is optional. A short course, remote helpdesk and site visit require different work; do not describe them as interchangeable.
Include the relevant advertising and computer-system arrangements, not just the training programme. General sales language should match the disclosure and agreements.

sections.heading: Can the home team deliver the U.S. promise?
paragraphs: A European support manager may already cover the home network during European hours. If you promise U.S. field support, establish who can handle urgent questions, travel or cover absences, and how that work will be funded.
If those resources do not exist, address the gap before selling the promise. The disclosure does not impose one staffing model or service frequency on every foreign brand.

practicalOutput: Compare each significant support promise with the people, time and budget that can deliver it.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Specified preopening/continuing assistance, advertising, computer systems/training and agreement references.
Conditional/optional distinctions and no inventedfrequency/staffmodel.
Actual delivery resources separate from disclosure promise.

title: FDD Item 12: what does the exclusive territory include?
seoTitle: FDD Item 12: Franchise Territory and Exclusivity
description: Read a territory promise alongside reserved channels, competition and the conditions for keeping or expanding the territory.
learningSummary: Before promising a U.S. partner an exclusive territory, decide which customers and sales channels it includes. Your brand may retain national accounts inside that area. The map alone does not allocate the sale, work or revenue.

sections.heading: Read the rights behind the boundary
paragraphs: Item 12 covers location and territory, exclusivity and its conditions, relocation or additional rights, reserved channels and relevant competing operations. Read what protection is offered, what the brand retains and what conditions keep the right in place.
A private territory arrangement does not stop every unrelated competitor from trading nearby.

sections.heading: A national customer can cross the local area
paragraphs: Suppose a Dutch business-services brand keeps a national customer with sites inside its U.S. operator’s territory. Establish who may sell to that customer, who must serve the sites and who invoices or receives the revenue.
Make the Item 12 explanation, agreement and operating instructions describe the same allocation. Do not rely on a verbal assurance that “the territory is protected.”

practicalOutput: Resolve retained accounts and channels before setting the territory promise or estimating the operator’s revenue.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Location/territory/exclusivityconditions, relocation/additional rights, reservedchannels/relevantcompetingoperations.
Private rights not universal government exclusion of competitors.
Sales/service/revenueallocation follows actualterms; no automatic exclusivity.

title: FDD Item 13: can the seller grant the brand rights?
seoTitle: FDD Item 13: Trademarks, Ownership and U.S. Rights
description: Item 13 explains the principal trademarks, relevant U.S. status, material disputes and the terms for protection or replacement.
learningSummary: The offering company needs to explain the principal trademarks and relevant U.S. status. A familiar home-country name does not settle the rights the U.S. seller and operators can use.

sections.heading: Identify the mark, owner and permission
paragraphs: If a group company owns the brand, check the arrangement allowing the seller and operators to use it. The mark owner and franchise seller are not interchangeable simply because they share a parent.

Item 13 addresses principal marks, registration or application status, relevant disputes, limits and protection responsibilities. Read the terms about protecting or changing the mark as well as its recorded status.

sections.heading: Registration and clearance answer different questions
paragraphs: A registration or application record does not replace checking the intended U.S. use and relevant competing rights. Nor does a home-country certificate decide that U.S. question.
Obtain the relevant clearance assessment and permission for the proposed use before relying on the group’s history. None of these records guarantees that a challenge will never arise.

practicalOutput: Check the relevant U.S. position and the seller’s permission to grant use, including the stated protection and change arrangements.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Principalmarks/status/disputes/limits/protection/changeprovisions.
Actualowner/seller/operator permissionsdistinct; registrationnotclearance and no mandatoryregistrationclaim.
Homecountryrights notsettleUSposition; no guaranteechallengefree.

title: FDD Item 14: can operators use your manuals, videos and software?
seoTitle: FDD Item 14: Patents, Copyright and Proprietary Information
description: An operating system can combine material you own with material licensed from someone else.
learningSummary: An operating system can combine material you own with material licensed from someone else. Item 14 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) addresses relevant patents, copyright and confidential proprietary information, including important rights and limits.

sections.heading: Check each essential component
paragraphs: A training package might contain a staff-written manual, commissioned videos and a supplier’s platform. Ownership of the manual does not establish permission for every component.

Check who owns each important part and whether the permission covers the proposed U.S. operators, use, territory and duration. A supplier licence can have different limits from material your business created.

sections.heading: Explain material rights and restrictions
paragraphs: The item addresses material patent/copyright rights and applications, relevant limits or proceedings, protection obligations and the general nature of confidential proprietary information. The complete prescribed item supplies its required detail.
An intellectual-property permission does not settle independent customer-data or privacy duties. Keep that separate question with the actual information being shared.

practicalOutput: Check that the rights behind the actual training and systems package cover the operator use you propose to sell.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Materialpatent/copyrightrights/applications/limits/proceedings/protectionobligations; generalnatureconfidentialinformation.
Ownershipversuspermissionwithuser/country/activity/durationlimits.
Manual/video/platformexample notownershipfinding; dataprivacyindependent.

title: FDD Item 15: can the operator hire a manager?
seoTitle: FDD Item 15: Owner Participation and Manager-Run Franchises
description: Your FDD must explain the operator’s personal participation obligations and whether you recommend participation.
learningSummary: Your Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) must explain the operator’s personal participation obligations and whether you recommend participation. If you offer a manager-run business, describe the actual requirements—including those imposed in practice, not just in the written agreement.

sections.heading: When on-site supervision by the owner is not required
paragraphs: Where personal on-premises supervision is not required, Item 15 asks for the following information about the operator (the franchisee). These questions describe your offer; they are not conditions shared by every franchise.
bullets: For an individual franchisee, whether you recommend that individual’s on-premises supervision.
Limits on whom the franchisee may hire as the on-premises supervisor.
Whether that supervisor must successfully complete your training programme.
For a company or other business-entity franchisee, the ownership share (equity), if any, the supervisor must hold in the operating business.

sections.heading: Explain manager restrictions separately
paragraphs: Item 15 also requires disclosure of restrictions the operator must impose on its manager, such as confidentiality or a stated noncompetition restriction. That duty is not limited to the no-personal-supervision situation. Disclosure does not establish whether a restriction is enforceable under other applicable law.

sections.heading: Check the job you are promising can be staffed
paragraphs: For example, an owner staying in Singapore may plan to hire a U.S. manager. Check the actual training, ownership and replacement conditions before assuming any experienced employee can cover an absence. Budget salary, employer costs, benefits and backup cover. Permission to use a manager does not pay for one; employment and work-permission questions remain separate.

practicalOutput: Before describing the offer as manager-run, make the participation, supervisor and replacement conditions match the operation you will actually support.
limitations: This explains the federal disclosure item, not whether a particular staffing arrangement or manager restriction is permitted under every applicable law.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Personal participation obligation and recommendation; written agreements AND franchisor practice.
Exact no-personal-on-premises-supervision condition for individual recommendation, hiring limits, successful training and entity equity questions.
Separate manager-restriction disclosure not confined to that branch; enforceability remains independent.
Manager cost, backup and independent employment/immigration questions.

title: FDD Item 16: can the operator add another service?
seoTitle: FDD Item 16: Products, Services and Customer Restrictions
description: Brand permission covers the goods, services and customers allowed by the arrangement.
learningSummary: Brand permission covers the goods, services and customers allowed by the arrangement. Item 16 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) explains relevant restrictions and required offerings; it is not permission to add any related activity.

sections.heading: Read the authorised range
paragraphs: Check the permitted or required offerings, customer restrictions and the franchisor’s rights to change the range. A broad category such as facilities services can leave the actual tasks unclear.

sections.heading: A cleaning offer may not include mechanical work
paragraphs: If an operator wants to add mechanical maintenance, first compare those tasks with the agreement’s service range and customer conditions. Then check the separate qualifications or government permissions for the actual work and location.

The brand’s approval does not supply those qualifications. A government qualification does not by itself expand the private agreement either. Keep revenue from an unresolved service identified as an assumption.

practicalOutput: Confirm the actual service and customer permissions before treating the added work as part of the operator’s offer.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Goods/services/customerrestrictions, required offeringsandrightstochangerange.
Privatepermissionandpublicqualificationdistinct; uncertainrevenuenotconfirmed.

title: FDD Item 17: renewal, transfer and leaving the relationship
seoTitle: FDD Item 17: Renewal, Termination, Transfer and Disputes
description: Item 17 summarises renewal, termination, transfer, noncompetition and dispute terms. The actual agreement and applicable state protections determine their effect.
learningSummary: Opening is only the start of the agreement. Item 17 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) summarises specified relationship terms and points to the actual contract provisions for renewal, termination, transfer, restrictions and disputes.

sections.heading: Choose the event before reading its terms
paragraphs: Read the full referenced clause for the actual conditions, steps and consequences. The following events are different.

headers: Question to answer from the actual agreement
rows: Expiry or renewal
What happens at the end of the stated term, and what conditions apply to another term?
Early termination
What grounds, notice or other steps and consequences does the clause specify?
Transfer
What consent and other conditions apply to the proposed ownership change?
Noncompetition or disputes
What restrictions on competing work or dispute procedures apply, and what independent legal protections must also be checked?

sections.heading: Disclosure does not settle enforceability
paragraphs: A successful operator cannot assume renewal is automatic or a sale is unrestricted. Equally, disclosure of a clause does not establish it can be enforced in every state or remove a non-waivable protection.
Check the law applicable to the actual relationship before relying on a restriction or exit route. There is no single nationwide notice or cure timetable supplied by this item.

practicalOutput: Identify the proposed event and read its actual clause, then check the independent state protections that could affect it.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Specifiedterm/renewal/termination/transfer/noncompetition/disputearrangementswithcontractreferences.
Expiry/renewal/earlytermination/transferdistinctevents.
Independentnonwaivablestateprotections/enforceabilityandnouniversaltimeline.

title: FDD Item 18: public figures promoting the franchise
seoTitle: FDD Item 18: Public Figures, Benefits and Management Roles
description: Item 18 addresses specified public-figure arrangements connected with the franchise offer.
learningSummary: Item 18 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) addresses specified public-figure arrangements connected with the franchise offer. Explain the person’s actual role and benefits instead of relying on a familiar name in recruitment material.

sections.heading: Identify the arrangement
paragraphs: The item covers compensation or benefits given or promised for public-figure use in the franchise name or symbol, or for endorsing or recommending the franchise to prospective operators. It also addresses relevant management involvement and investment, including the stated value of services.

A public figure can be generally known in the area of the proposed franchise; the definition is not limited to international celebrities. Ordinary consumer advertising should not automatically be treated as franchise-offer promotion.

sections.heading: Separate promotion from delivery
paragraphs: If a presenter appears in recruitment material, state what that person actually does. Promotion, investment and managing training are different roles.
Use the assistance disclosures for support promises and the financial disclosures for financial claims. The public figure’s visibility does not supply that evidence.

practicalOutput: Make recruitment statements match the actual public-figure arrangement and the disclosures about role, benefits and involvement.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
editNote: Replaced the repeated introduction/example/quiz/checklist stack with an owner-first explanation and retained material disclosure conditions.
conditionsRetained: Definedlocalpublicfigure; coveredname/symbol/franchiseendorsementuses and compensation/benefits.
Management/investment/valueofservices; ordinaryconsumeradnotautomaticallysamearrangement.
Noendorsementasperformance/supportevidence.

title: FDD Item 19: what can you say about earnings?
seoTitle: FDD Item 19: Financial Performance Representations and Earnings
description: What sales and earnings figures leave out, what Item 19 requires, and why a buyer must compare the costs and operators behind a claim.
learningSummary: A sales figure does not show what the operator keeps after costs. Item 19 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) sets disclosure requirements for sales and earnings claims. Before using a figure, know what it measures, whose businesses it describes and which costs it leaves out.

sections.heading: Choose whether to make an earnings claim
paragraphs: A financial performance representation is a statement about financial results or potential results covered by the rule. You may choose not to make one, but Item 19 still has to be addressed. Where you make a representation, it needs a reasonable basis and written substantiation—the material supporting the claim—when made, and must appear in Item 19 with the required supporting detail and qualifications.

Written support alone does not permit a salesperson to make an earnings claim orally, in an advertisement or on a separate spreadsheet. The rule has specific, conditional treatment for actual records of an existing outlet being considered for purchase and properly identified supplemental representations; these are not general permission for off-document claims.

sections.heading: What changes when the U.S. unit pays a manager?
paragraphs: Fictional example: a unit has $1,000,000 annual revenue and $180,000 remaining before two costs that have not yet been included—a manager and a royalty. Assume a complete manager cost of $120,000 and a royalty of 6% of revenue.

rows: Starting remainder before the two omitted costs
Manager cost
Left before any other omitted costs

sections.heading: Check the starting figure before subtracting
paragraphs: The example illustrates cost definitions, not a brand’s actual earnings. Do not deduct a manager or royalty twice if the starting figure already includes it. Check the source period, currency, units included and excluded, unit type and costs. Founder-operated, company-owned and franchised units can have different economics; an average can hide their differences. Projections also depend on their stated assumptions.
Keep your internal planning assumptions distinct from the figures and qualifications used in recruitment. Strong home-market sales alone do not describe a U.S. unit’s manager-inclusive result.

practicalOutput: Before using a financial figure in recruitment, check its definition and supporting basis and apply the required Item 19 treatment. The linked guide explains the home-market pitch problem.
limitations: The calculation is invented teaching material, not a real result or forecast. This covers selected federal requirements; state requirements and a particular representation need their own assessment.

title: FDD Item 20: what changed in the franchise network?
seoTitle: FDD Item 20: Outlets, Closures and Franchisee Information
description: An ending outlet total can hide openings, departures and ownership changes.
learningSummary: An ending outlet total can hide openings, departures and ownership changes. Item 20 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) provides prescribed outlet tables and specified current or former franchisee information to examine those changes.

sections.heading: Keep the population and period consistent
paragraphs: Read the actual headings, reporting periods and outlet types. Company-owned and franchised units are different groups. Termination, nonrenewal, transfer and closure are not interchangeable categories.
Net growth alone establishes neither operator success nor support quality. Use the described contacts and records to investigate the specific questions raised.

sections.heading: Net growth leaves important questions open
paragraphs: Fictional example: a counted population begins at 20 units, adds eight and has five leave it. It ends at 23, a net increase of three. The calculation does not say why the five left or whether the new units are performing as expected.

Check the real categories before interpreting departures; do not label them all failures or treat every transfer as an outlet closure. Growth also raises a separate question about the resources available to support the larger network.

practicalOutput: Read the period and categories before comparing totals, and use current/former operator information to investigate specific changes.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.

title: FDD Item 21: whose financial statements are you showing?
seoTitle: FDD Item 21: Financial Statements, Audits and Guarantees
description: The accounts must relate to the businesses required by Item 21, not simply the wealthiest company in the group.
learningSummary: The accounts must relate to the businesses required by Item 21 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD), not simply the wealthiest company in the group. A new U.S. seller cannot assume its parent’s accounts or home-country audit satisfy the offer’s requirements.

sections.heading: Start with the company and accounting basis
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies financial statements, audit standards and treatment of relevant affiliates, parents and subfranchisors. The rule addresses U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, or treatment permitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission, with the applicable audit requirements.

A balance sheet shows financial position at a date; an income statement covers performance over a period; a cash-flow statement explains cash movements. Check the named entity, dates, accountant’s report and notes before comparing figures.

sections.heading: Know which periods the ordinary rule covers
paragraphs: A fiscal year is the business’s accounting year, not necessarily the calendar year.

rows: Balance sheets
Previous two fiscal year-ends
Operations, stockholders’ equity and cash flows
Previous three fiscal years

sections.heading: An affiliate alternative needs the actual guarantee
paragraphs: The affiliate alternative requires compliant statements and an absolute, unconditional guarantee of all the franchisor’s obligations to the franchisee under the franchise agreement. The guarantee need not cover third parties, and a copy is attached to the disclosure.
Group ownership or a limited support letter is not that guarantee. Separate parent or subfranchisor statement requirements can also apply.

sections.heading: The start-up phase-in is conditional
paragraphs: A start-up franchise system without audited statements may use the limited phase-in. A newly formed U.S. seller does not qualify merely because it is new. Audited statements must be prepared as soon as practicable; the unaudited format must conform as closely as possible, with the required history or conspicuous shorter-history explanation.

headers: Selling stage described in the rule
rows: First partial or full fiscal year selling franchises
Unaudited opening balance sheet

Required statements for the previous fiscal year plus previously disclosed audited statements still required by the ordinary periods

sections.heading: Accounts and the support budget answer different questions
paragraphs: Past financial statements do not guarantee future support resources. Check the actual company commitments and cash available for training, systems, travel and field support. Do not treat every parent asset as cash available to its subsidiary.

practicalOutput: Establish the required reporting entities, periods, accounting basis and audit requirements with the responsible accountant before assembling the financial exhibits.
limitations: This explains the stated Item 21 periods and conditional alternatives. It does not decide current SEC acceptance of a particular foreign accounting treatment or establish that a start-up or guarantee route applies.

title: FDD Item 22: read the whole proposed agreement package
seoTitle: FDD Item 22: Contracts, Exhibits and Agreement Versions
description: The main franchise agreement may not contain every commitment in the offer.
learningSummary: The main franchise agreement may not contain every commitment in the offer. Item 22 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) attaches the proposed agreements covered by the offering requirements so related costs and obligations can be read together.

sections.heading: Check the terms outside the main contract
paragraphs: The prescribed item includes the franchise agreement and relevant lease, option or purchase agreements. The complete attachment requirements depend on the actual offering.

For example, the commercial email may agree a fee and territory while separate software terms and a guarantee create other commitments. Compare their parties, versions, costs and obligations with the promised deal; an attachment is not government approval.

sections.heading: A revised attachment can raise a timing question
paragraphs: If a guarantee, fee or other term changes later, compare the signing version with the package that was actually delivered. A tidy exhibit index does not settle whether the change creates a further disclosure or timing duty. Check that question before signature or payment.

practicalOutput: Read the connected agreements as one offer and identify any later difference before arranging signature or payment.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.

title: FDD Item 23: what the disclosure receipt records
seoTitle: FDD Item 23: Receipts and Disclosure Delivery Records
description: The receipt acknowledges the disclosure package.
learningSummary: The receipt acknowledges the disclosure package. It is different from the franchise agreement and does not show that the recipient accepted the investment, understood every term or waived rights.

sections.heading: Use the prescribed receipt
paragraphs: Item 23 requires two copies of the prescribed detachable acknowledgement as the last pages of the FDD. A homemade “information received” statement is not a substitute.

The receipt identifies the issuance date, exhibit titles and relevant franchise sellers’ names, principal business addresses and telephone numbers. It also addresses the registered agent’s name/address if not already disclosed as the rule specifies. It includes space for the prospective franchisee’s signature and date; return instructions are optional.

sections.heading: Match it to what was delivered
paragraphs: If two dated FDD files have circulated, establish the actual recipient, delivery date, document version and attachments. A signed receipt does not prove that a different version or omitted exhibit was supplied.
Check agreement/payment timing separately under applicable federal and state requirements. Preserve uncertain delivery facts until resolved rather than changing a date to fit the intended signing.

practicalOutput: Match the prescribed receipt to the actual delivered FDD and exhibits, then check the independent signing and payment timetable.
limitations: This explains the selected federal disclosure item. State and territorial requirements and the terms of the particular offer remain separate.
